Adding an RV or Boat Parking Pad in Florida: Size, Thickness and Rules

An RV or boat parking pad in Florida typically runs 12 to 14 ft wide and 26 to 51 ft long, poured 5 to 6 in thick depending on the vehicle's weight. As of October 2026, Florida market data puts a concrete slab at $4 to $10 per sq ft installed, and most jurisdictions in Greater Orlando and Sarasota-Manatee require a separate zoning or storage permit on top of the flatwork permit.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

How Big Should an RV or Boat Parking Pad Be?

Most residential RV pads run about 12 ft wide and anywhere from 26 ft long for a van-class rig to roughly 50 ft for a full Class A motorhome towing a car behind it, with 2 to 3 ft of clearance on each side so doors can open and a person can walk the length of the pad. A boat pad is sized to the trailer rather than the hull, usually 10 to 12 ft wide and as long as the boat and trailer tongue together, plus turning room if the driveway doesn't run straight to the street.

RV pad size by vehicle, rough guide
VehicleTypical pad size
Class B van (about 20 ft)12 ft × 26 ft
Class C motorhome (about 28 ft)12 ft × 34 ft
Class A plus a towed car (about 45 ft combined)14 ft × 51 ft

DrivewayzUSA, RV parking pad design; measure your own unit's length and width before ordering concrete, since models vary within each class.

Our concrete slabs page covers how we size and quote a utility pad once the vehicle's exact dimensions and the lot's access route are known; this guide focuses on the planning questions specific to parking an RV or a boat.

How Thick Does a Concrete RV or Boat Pad Need to Be?

Florida's residential code sets 3½ in as the bare floor for any ground-supported slab, but a pad carrying an RV or a loaded boat trailer is built well above that minimum (FBC Residential Ch. 5). A 5 in slab handles most RVs up to about 16,000 lb, and dual-axle trailers or a heavier Class A rig call for 6 in with reinforcement, the same step up driveways take once trucks and boat trailers are the regular load rather than daily cars (DrivewayzUSA). Florida market data for concrete slabs runs $4–$10 per sq ft installed, with thickness and base compaction, not square footage, doing most of the work to move that price up or down (HomeGuide; Angi Orlando).

Gravel, Pavers or Poured Concrete: Which Surface Holds Up Under an RV?

All three carry a parked RV or boat trailer, and the choice usually comes down to drainage, upkeep and whether the pad also needs to look finished from the street rather than purely functional.

RV and boat pad surfaces compared
SurfaceWhat it takes to hold the loadTrade-off
Poured concrete5 to 6 in, reinforced, on a compacted baseHighest upfront cost; least upkeep once it's down
Pavers80 mm (about 3⅛ in) units over a 6 in compacted aggregate base, the same step up driveways take for trucks and trailersA sunken corner can be lifted and reset rather than patched
Compacted gravelA crowned, well-drained base, deeper where soil is poorRuts and scatters under repeated turning; needs periodic regrading

ICPI Tech Spec 2, the construction standard for interlocking concrete pavements (ICPI Tech Spec 2).

Gravel is the cheapest way to get a vehicle off the lawn, but a tire turning sharply on loose stone tends to push it into ruts within a season or two, which is the main reason owners who keep an RV long-term move to a paved surface. Our paver driveway page covers the base build in more depth for a pad that doubles as extra driveway parking rather than a standalone slab.

Does a Florida HOA Have to Allow an RV or Boat Pad?

Not automatically, and most master-planned communities in both service areas restrict where a recreational vehicle or boat can sit in plain view, even on an improved pad. Florida law protects what an owner stores only where it can't be seen: an association may not restrict items, including a boat or an RV, that aren't visible from the parcel's frontage, an adjacent parcel or an adjacent common area, which is why most approved RV pads sit behind a fence, a hedge or the side of the house rather than in the open front driveway (F.S. 720.3045).

Manatee County's own zoning rule follows the same logic on the government side: a restricted vehicle, its definition covers boats and RVs, can sit in a side or rear yard without extending more than 5 ft past the front of the house, or in a front yard only on a corner lot's secondary frontage, set back 10 ft and screened behind a fence or hedge at least 6 ft tall (Manatee County Land Development Code). Sarasota County's rule caps the count rather than the visibility: an operational, currently tagged RV or boat owned by the resident can be stored outside, up to two per lot, without the same screening requirement (Sarasota County Zoning Code, Appendix A §7.1). Our HOA approval guide covers the paperwork side of getting a pad approved before it's poured.

Does an RV or Boat Pad Need a County Permit?

Often yes, and the permit frequently covers the vehicle itself as well as the pad underneath it, not just the concrete work. Orange County requires a Boat, Recreational Vehicle or Temporary Portable Storage Container permit under its zoning code, separate from any building permit for the slab, with a $47 fee, a site plan showing the setback from each property line, and a photo and registration for the vehicle being stored; installing pavers or another improved surface for the pad needs its own sign-off as part of that application (Orange County, Boat/RV storage permit). A plain slab pour over $2,500 also triggers Florida's lien-law Notice of Commencement, recorded before work starts regardless of whether the local zoning permit is separate (F.S. 713.13). Requirements vary enough between cities and counties that a call to the local zoning office before ordering concrete is worth it; our Orange County permit guide and our Sarasota County permit guide cover the flatwork side of that process.

How Do You Keep Water From Pooling Around an RV or Boat Pad?

A pad built flat, or worse, sloped toward the house, holds rainwater against tires and the base long enough to soften the ground underneath over a few wet seasons. We grade an RV or boat pad with a slight crown or a consistent slope away from the house and any structure nearby, carrying water to the same swale or yard drain the rest of the lot already uses rather than creating a new low spot. On flatwoods soils with a seasonal water table that can sit within about 18 in of the surface for part of most years, Myakka among them, that slope matters more than it would on excessively drained ridge sand (NRCS, Myakka series).

Say You're Adding a Pad for a 32-Foot Travel Trailer in a Kissimmee Subdivision

A homeowner in a 1990s Kissimmee subdivision with a 32-foot trailer first checks the HOA declaration for a screening requirement, since the pad is going in the side yard behind a six-foot fence to stay clear of the frontage visibility rule. The pad itself comes in around 14 by 40 ft, poured at 5 in with wire mesh, graded to shed water toward the existing side-yard swale rather than back toward the house. Osceola County's driveway permit process covers the pad since it's new impervious construction, and the HOA's own architectural form goes in alongside it so both approvals move at the same time instead of one waiting on the other. Our Osceola County permit guide walks through what that application packet typically includes.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a permit for an RV or boat parking pad in Florida?

Often, and the permit can cover the vehicle as well as the pad. Orange County, for example, requires its own Boat, RV and Temporary Portable Storage Container permit in addition to any permit the concrete or paver work needs, with a site plan showing the setback from each property line. Rules differ enough by city and county that confirming with the local zoning office before pouring is worth the call.

Can an HOA stop a resident from parking an RV or boat in the driveway?

Usually, if it's visible from the street or a neighboring lot. Florida law only protects items that aren't visible from the parcel's frontage or an adjacent parcel, which is why most approved pads sit behind a fence or on the side of the house rather than in an open front driveway.

How thick should a concrete RV pad be?

Five inches handles most RVs up to about 16,000 lb; dual-axle trailers or a heavier Class A motorhome call for 6 inches with reinforcement. That's the same step up a driveway takes once it carries trucks or boat trailers instead of daily cars.

Is gravel an acceptable surface for an RV or boat pad?

It can be for a short-term or budget setup, but loose gravel tends to rut where a vehicle turns sharply, which usually means regrading every season or two. Concrete or pavers over a compacted base hold up longer under repeated turning and braking.

How big should an RV parking pad be?

Most residential pads run about 12 to 14 ft wide and 26 to 51 ft long depending on the RV class, with 2 to 3 ft of clearance on each side. Measuring the specific unit's length and width, rather than going by its class alone, avoids ordering a pad that's a few feet short.
